.engramdb/memories/enqueueing-background-jobs_01a10c2d-e3c1-7253-9b3d-2e1bc5c7fa0f.md:15:Enqueue background work with `src.jobs.queue.enqueue(name, payload, dedupe_key=...)`. Job names are `<domain>.<verb>` (e.g. `invoices.send_reminder`); payloads are JSON with ids only, never objects. Always pass a `dedupe_key` derived from the business key (e.g. `f"dunning:{invoice_id}:{attempt}"`): webhooks and cron both redeliver, and the backend drops a job whose dedupe_key it has seen in the last 7 days.

Emails from the notifier now go out with a From address. In `services/notifier/notifier/provider.py` I added a `FROM_ADDR = "receipts@mail.acme.example"` constant and `send()` now includes `"from": FROM_ADDR` in the request it sends to the email provider. The notifier's test suite passes, though its one test mocks out `send()`, so nothing exercises the new field yet.

I took the address from the project's memory notes. They say the `mail.` subdomain has its own SPF and DMARC records, and that mail from the bare `acme.example` domain started landing in spam in September 2026. The notes also list two older sender addresses, `billing@acme.example` and `noreply@acme.example`. Both are marked as replaced, so I didn't use either.

One item:

- **A way to see the whole supersession chain, e.g. a `lineage` / `history` tool, or a `follow_supersession: true` parameter on `get`.** There were three memories about the sender address: `billing@acme.example`, `noreply@acme.example` (2025) and `receipts@mail.acme.example` (current). `get` on the `billing@` memory showed only one step, `superseded_by` the `noreply@` (2025) memory. It didn't show that this one had in turn been replaced by the "(current)" memory. To be sure `receipts@mail.acme.example` was the newest version, I had to piece the chain together myself from grep hits over `.engramdb/memories/` plus the hook's injected memory. One call that returns the full chain from oldest to newest, with the `invalidated_at` date of each step, would have confirmed this directly. A smaller fix that would also have worked: have `get` on an invalidated memory include the id of the current end of its chain, not just the next step.
